idiom_name: net/rpc client (forwarder) + registered receiver methods (receiver), gob on the wire
implementation_notes: Go ships the pattern as net/rpc: rpc.Dial returns a client whose typed Call gob-encodes the arguments and writes them to the connection (the forwarder), while rpc.Register plus rpc.Accept on the peer side unmarshal a request and invoke the named exported method (the receiver) - no envelope, framing or dispatch table is written by hand. The package is frozen and will not receive new features, so new code usually keeps the shape and replaces the halves: a length-prefixed loop over net.Conn with encoding/gob or encoding/json and a map of handlers, or a schema-driven stack such as gRPC/connect. The classic structure survives as the two halves; what disappears is the marshalling boilerplate and the argument (de)serialisation.
pitfalls: gob omits zero values, so a zero-length field is indistinguishable from 'not sent'; both sides must also register identical concrete types or decoding fails.
client.Call blocks with no deadline - a dead peer hangs until the kernel gives up - so use Go() with a done channel and your own context timeout.
net.Conn writes are not message-delimited; anything built by hand needs explicit framing (or net/rpc, which supplies it).
